library(tidyverse)

**GitHub repository:** https://github.com/namanjain2404/bos-flight-delays

## Abstract

Flight delays impose substantial costs on airlines, airports and passengers,
and departures from congested hubs such as Boston Logan International Airport
(BOS) are exposed both to weather and to delays that build up over the day.
This project set out to describe when and why departures from BOS are
delayed, to measure how much weather increases the risk of a delay, and to
predict delays before departure. We combined official U.S. on-time records
for all 144,174 scheduled BOS departures between September 2025 and August
2026 with hourly weather observations at the airport. About one in four
operated departures left at least 15 minutes late, and the risk rose sharply
over the day, from under 10% in the early morning to over 40% in the evening.
Precipitation increased the delay rate from 22% to 36%, an effect that
remained after accounting for time of day, season and airline. Machine
learning models trained on earlier months identified about half of the
delayed flights in the following summer, with a simple regularized logistic
regression performing almost as well as gradient-boosted trees. The time of
day was by far the most important predictor.

\newpage

# Introduction

A flight is officially considered delayed when it departs 15 or more minutes
after its scheduled time. Delays are costly for airlines (crew and aircraft
schedules), for airports (gate and runway congestion) and for passengers
(missed connections and lost time). Boston Logan is a busy hub in a region
with frequent rain, fog and winter storms, so both weather and the knock-on
effect of earlier delays are plausible drivers of departure delays. Knowing
which flights are most at risk, and how strongly weather matters, can help
travelers choose flights and help airlines and airports plan resources.

The **domain problem** is to understand and anticipate departure delays at
BOS. We translated it into three **analytic problems**: (1) describe how the
share of delayed departures varies with the time of day, season, airline and
the causes reported for delays; (2) test whether weather at the departure
hour (precipitation, snow, fog, low visibility and wind) is associated with a
higher delay rate, before and after adjusting for time of day, month and
airline; and (3) build and evaluate classifiers that predict whether a
departure will be delayed by 15 or more minutes using only information
available before departure.

# Methods

## Data collection and storage

Flight data come from the Bureau of Transportation Statistics (BTS) Reporting
Carrier On-Time Performance table [1], which records every domestic flight of
the major U.S. carriers, including scheduled and actual times, delay causes,
cancellations and diversions. We downloaded the twelve monthly national files
for September 2025 to August 2026 with an R script and kept only departures
from BOS, giving 144,174 scheduled departures by 12 carriers. Weather data
come from NOAA's Local Climatological Data version 2 (LCDv2) [2] for the
Boston Logan station (USW00014739). We used only the routine hourly reports
(report type FM-15, issued at about 54 minutes past each hour) and extracted
temperature, dew point, relative humidity, visibility, wind speed and gusts,
precipitation, the cloud ceiling, and indicators for rain, snow, fog or mist
and thunderstorms from the present-weather codes. Non-numeric codes required
recoding: "T" (trace precipitation) was treated as no measurable amount but
kept as a separate flag, and quality flags appended to values were removed.

All data were stored in a SQLite database with separate tables for flights,
hourly weather, carriers and destination airports, and joined with a SQL
query. Joining required care with time zones: BTS times are local clock
times that follow daylight saving time, whereas NOAA reports all times in
local standard time (UTC-5) all year, which we verified from the original
weather report time stamps. We therefore converted each scheduled departure
to local standard time and attached the weather report from just before the
scheduled departure hour. Of the 8,761 hours in the study period, 178 had no
hourly report; short gaps were filled with the previous hour's conditions,
but a gap in NOAA's data from August 29 to September 2, 2025 left 646 flights
(0.45%) without weather, and these were excluded from the weather analysis
and models. Cancelled (3.05%) and diverted flights have no valid departure
delay and were analyzed separately, leaving 138,743 operated departures with
weather for the delay analysis. BTS stores the minutes attributed to five
delay causes in separate columns, which we reshaped to a long format to
compare causes.

## Statistical inference

We compared the delay rate between departures with and without precipitation
with a two-sample test of proportions and a 95% confidence interval for the
difference, and tested whether delay rates differ between carriers with a
chi-square test of independence (alpha = 0.05). Because weather is correlated
with time of day and season, we also fitted a logistic regression for the
probability of a delay with indicators for precipitation, snow, fog or mist
and visibility below 5 km, wind speed, five departure-time blocks, month and
carrier, and report adjusted odds ratios with 95% Wald confidence intervals.

## Predictive modeling

The prediction target was whether an operated departure was delayed by 15 or
more minutes. Predictors were limited to information known before departure:
scheduled hour, day of week, carrier, destination, distance, days to the
nearest federal holiday (capped at 7), and the weather variables described
above at the scheduled departure hour. To reflect real use, we used a
time-based split, training on September 2025 to May 2026 (101,238 flights,
23.3% delayed) and testing on June to August 2026 (37,505 flights, 26.6%
delayed). Month was therefore excluded, since the test months do not occur in
the training data. Rare carriers and destinations were pooled, categorical
variables were dummy-encoded and numeric variables standardized.

We compared a majority-class baseline, lasso (L1-regularized) logistic
regression, a random forest (300 trees) and gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost,
500 trees), implemented with tidymodels [3] and the glmnet [4], ranger [5] and
xgboost [6] packages. Hyperparameters (the lasso penalty, the number of
variables per split and minimum node size of the forest, and the tree depth
and learning rate of XGBoost) were tuned by 5-fold cross-validation on the
training data using ROC-AUC. The folds were **grouped by date**, so all
flights from the same day were in the same fold. Flights on the same day
share the same weather and disruptions, and an initial analysis with random
folds produced cross-validated ROC-AUC values of about 0.78 for the tree
models that did not hold up on the test data. Each tuned model was refit on
the full training data and evaluated once on the test months using ROC-AUC
and the area under the precision-recall curve (PR-AUC), which is more
informative than accuracy when delays are the minority class. We also report
precision and recall at probability thresholds of 0.5 and 0.3.

# Results

## When and why departures are delayed

Overall, 24.2% of operated departures left at least 15 minutes late. The
strongest pattern was the time of day (Figure 1): the delay rate rose almost
steadily from 6.7% at 5:00 to 43.9% at 19:00 and stayed above 40% through the
evening. This pattern is consistent with the reported causes of delay, since
late-arriving aircraft accounted for 46.9% of all delay minutes, followed by
carrier causes (30.3%) and the National Aviation System (20.0%), while
extreme weather accounted for only 2.7% (Appendix, Figure 5). Delay rates
also varied by season, with the highest rates in July (30.2%) and August
(27.9%), and by carrier: among the large carriers, rates ranged from 19.0%
for United to 36.2% for Southwest and 38.0% for Spirit, and the differences
between carriers were highly significant (chi-square = 1639.9, df = 11,
p < 0.001; Appendix, Figure 4).

```{r fig-hour, fig.cap = "Share of operated BOS departures delayed by 15 or more minutes by scheduled departure hour (September 2025 to August 2026). Point size shows the number of departures; hours with fewer than 100 departures are omitted."}
op %>%
  group_by(crs_dep_hour) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), rate = mean(dep_del15)) %>%
  filter(n >= 100) %>%
  ggplot(aes(crs_dep_hour, rate)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = "#2c7fb8") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(5, 22, by = 2)) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5, labels = comma) +
  labs(x = "Scheduled departure hour (local time)",
       y = "Delayed 15+ min", size = "Departures")
```

## Effect of weather

Every adverse weather condition at the scheduled departure hour was
associated with a higher delay rate (Figure 2). Departures during
precipitation were delayed 36.3% of the time compared with 22.2% in dry
conditions, a difference of 14.1 percentage points (95% CI 13.4 to 14.9;
p < 0.001). The rate was 42.7% during snow and 38.9% during fog or mist. In
the logistic regression adjusting for time of day, month and carrier,
precipitation increased the odds of a delay by 80% (odds ratio 1.80, 95% CI
1.73 to 1.88), with further increases for snow (1.36), fog or mist (1.51),
visibility below 5 km (1.15) and each additional meter per second of wind
(1.03); all were significant (Appendix, Table 2).

```{r fig-weather, fig.height = 2.6, fig.cap = "Delay rate of operated BOS departures when each weather condition was or was not present at the scheduled departure hour, with 95\\% confidence intervals."}
conditions <- c(any_precip = "Any precipitation", rain = "Rain",
                snow = "Snow", fog_mist = "Fog or mist",
                low_vis = "Visibility < 5 km", strong_wind = "Wind >= 10 m/s")

op %>%
  mutate(low_vis = as.integer(visibility_km < 5),
         strong_wind = as.integer(wind_speed_ms >= 10)) %>%
  select(dep_del15, all_of(names(conditions))) %>%
  pivot_longer(-dep_del15, names_to = "condition", values_to = "present") %>%
  group_by(condition, present) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), rate = mean(dep_del15), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n),
         condition = factor(conditions[condition], levels = rev(conditions)),
         present = if_else(present == 1, "Present", "Absent")) %>%
  ggplot(aes(rate, condition, colour = present)) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = rate - 1.96 * se, xmax = rate + 1.96 * se),
                 height = 0.25) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c(Absent = "grey50", Present = "#d95f02")) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Delayed 15+ min", y = NULL, colour = "Condition")
```

## Predicting delays

All three models clearly outperformed the baseline on the test months
(Table 1, Figure 3). XGBoost achieved the highest ROC-AUC (0.745) and PR-AUC
(0.543, about twice the no-skill value of 0.266), but the lasso logistic
regression was almost as good (ROC-AUC 0.743), and the random forest was
slightly weaker (0.733). With date-grouped folds, the cross-validated ROC-AUC
on the training months (0.723 to 0.742) closely matched the test results. At
the default threshold of 0.5, the models flagged few flights (recall of 10.5%
for the lasso and 30.0% for XGBoost). At a threshold of 0.3, XGBoost detected
53.4% of the delayed departures (5,318 of 9,968) with a precision of 50.7%.
Its accuracy of 73.8% was barely above the 73.4% obtained by always
predicting "on time", which illustrates why accuracy is not a useful measure
here. The scheduled departure hour was by far the most important predictor,
accounting for roughly 40% of XGBoost's total gain, followed by relative
humidity, temperature, dew point, visibility and distance (Appendix,
Figure 6).

```{r tab-models}
res$test_preds %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  summarise(roc_auc = roc_auc_vec(delayed, .pred_delayed),
            pr_auc = pr_auc_vec(delayed, .pred_delayed)) %>%
  mutate(pr_auc = if_else(model == "Baseline", res$test_delay_rate, pr_auc)) %>%
  left_join(res$cv %>% select(model, cv_auc = mean), by = "model") %>%
  arrange(desc(roc_auc)) %>%
  select(model, cv_auc, roc_auc, pr_auc) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
               col.names = c("Model", "CV ROC-AUC (training)",
                             "Test ROC-AUC", "Test PR-AUC"),
               caption = paste("Cross-validated (grouped by date) and test",
                               "performance; test period June to August 2026."))
```

```{r fig-roc, fig.height = 3, fig.width = 4.5, out.width = "65%", fig.cap = "ROC curves of the three models on the test months (June to August 2026). The dashed line corresponds to the baseline."}
res$test_preds %>%
  filter(model != "Baseline") %>%
  group_by(model) %>%
  roc_curve(delayed, .pred_delayed) %>%
  ggplot(aes(1 - specificity, sensitivity, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey60") +
  geom_path(linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_equal() +
  labs(x = "False positive rate", y = "True positive rate", colour = NULL)
```

# Discussion

The project answered its three questions. Departure delays at BOS are driven
mainly by when a flight is scheduled: the risk of a delay increases more than
sixfold from the first departures of the morning to the evening, and almost
half of all delay minutes come from aircraft arriving late from earlier
flights. For travelers, the practical implication is simple: early-morning
departures are by far the most reliable. For airlines and the airport, the
results point to delay propagation as the main lever, for example through
larger schedule buffers in the afternoon and evening. Weather matters as
well: precipitation, snow, fog and low visibility each raise the delay rate
substantially, even after accounting for time of day, season and airline,
although BTS attributes only 2.7% of delay minutes to "extreme weather". This
suggests that most weather-related delays are recorded under the National
Aviation System category, so the official cause categories understate the
role of everyday weather.

The predictive models showed that delays are only partly predictable from
information available before departure: the best model detects about half of
the delayed flights, and about half of its warnings are correct. Such a model
could support decisions where moderate accuracy is useful, such as
prioritizing passenger notifications or staffing on high-risk days, but it
would not be reliable enough to inform individual passengers with certainty.
The finding that a regularized logistic regression performs almost as well
as gradient-boosted trees indicates that most of the predictable signal is
captured by a few simple relationships, which favors the interpretable
model. Methodologically, the comparison of random and date-grouped
cross-validation shows that flights on the same day cannot be treated as
independent observations, a point that applies to any model evaluated on
such data.

The study has several limitations. The models do not use the delay of the
inbound aircraft, even though late-arriving aircraft cause almost half of
all delay minutes; linking each departure to the previous flight of the same
aircraft through its tail number is the most promising extension. Weather is
measured only at BOS, not at the destination or elsewhere in the national
system. Month could not be used as a predictor with a time-based split, and
the summer test months had more delays than the training months. Finally,
the analysis covers one airport and one year, so the results may not
generalize to other airports or years with different schedules.

# Statement of contributions

- **Naman Jain:** collected the BTS flight data and wrote the download and
  filtering scripts, built the SQLite database and the SQL join of flights
  and weather, and set up the GitHub repository.
- **Yash Rahul Kava:** proposed the project topic, drafted the project
  proposal, researched background information on flight delays, and wrote
  the Introduction.
- **Sanket Kothari:** obtained and cleaned the NOAA weather data, handled the
  time-zone alignment between flights and weather, wrote the Methods section,
  and tested the reproducibility of the analysis.
- **Jinam Shah:** carried out the exploratory data analysis and the
  statistical inference (tests of proportions, chi-square test and logistic
  regression), created the corresponding figures, and wrote the Results
  section.
- **Sai Rishin Bussa:** built and tuned the predictive models, evaluated them
  on the test period (ROC and precision-recall analysis, decision thresholds
  and feature importance), and wrote the Discussion.

All team members reviewed the final report and presented in the in-class
presentation.

# Appendix

```{r fig-carrier, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Delay rate by carrier with 95\\% confidence intervals (carriers with at least 500 operated BOS departures). The dashed line marks the overall rate."}
op %>%
  group_by(carrier_name) %>%
  summarise(n = n(), rate = mean(dep_del15)) %>%
  filter(n >= 500) %>%
  mutate(se = sqrt(rate * (1 - rate) / n),
         carrier_name = fct_reorder(carrier_name, rate)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(rate, carrier_name)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = mean(op$dep_del15), linetype = "dashed",
             colour = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = rate - 1.96 * se, xmax = rate + 1.96 * se),
                 height = 0.3, colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(colour = "#2c7fb8", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Delayed 15+ min", y = NULL)
```

```{r fig-causes, fig.height = 2.2, fig.cap = "Share of delay minutes by cause for delayed BOS departures, as reported to BTS."}
fw %>%
  filter(cancelled == 0, dep_del15 == 1) %>%
  select(carrier_delay, weather_delay, nas_delay, security_delay,
         late_aircraft_delay) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "cause", values_to = "minutes") %>%
  group_by(cause) %>%
  summarise(minutes = sum(minutes, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%
  mutate(share = minutes / sum(minutes),
         cause = recode(cause, carrier_delay = "Carrier",
                        weather_delay = "Extreme weather",
                        nas_delay = "National Aviation System",
                        security_delay = "Security",
                        late_aircraft_delay = "Late-arriving aircraft"),
         cause = fct_reorder(cause, share)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(share, cause)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c7fb8", width = 0.6) +
  geom_text(aes(label = percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), hjust = -0.15,
            size = 3) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = percent_format(accuracy = 1),
                     limits = c(0, 0.55)) +
  labs(x = "Share of delay minutes", y = NULL)
```

```{r fig-importance, fig.height = 3.2, fig.cap = "Top 15 predictors of the XGBoost model by share of total gain."}
feature_labels <- c(
  crs_dep_hour = "Scheduled departure hour", rel_humidity = "Relative humidity",
  temp_c = "Temperature", dew_point_c = "Dew point",
  visibility_km = "Visibility", distance = "Distance",
  days_to_holiday = "Days to holiday", wind_speed_ms = "Wind speed",
  wind_gust_ms = "Wind gust", precip_mm = "Precipitation amount",
  any_precip = "Any precipitation", rain = "Rain", snow = "Snow",
  fog_mist = "Fog or mist", thunder = "Thunderstorm")

res$importance %>%
  slice_max(Gain, n = 15) %>%
  mutate(Feature = case_when(
    Feature %in% names(feature_labels) ~ feature_labels[Feature],
    str_detect(Feature, "^carrier_") ~
      paste("Carrier:", str_remove(Feature, "^carrier_")),
    str_detect(Feature, "^day_of_week_") ~
      paste("Day:", str_remove(Feature, "^day_of_week_")),
    str_detect(Feature, "^dest_") ~
      paste("Destination:", str_remove(Feature, "^dest_")),
    TRUE ~ Feature)) %>%
  ggplot(aes(Gain, fct_reorder(Feature, Gain))) +
  geom_col(fill = "#2c7fb8", width = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Share of total gain", y = NULL)
```

```{r tab-logit}
logit_data <- op %>%
  mutate(hour_block = cut(crs_dep_hour, breaks = c(0, 9, 12, 15, 18, 24),
                          right = FALSE),
         month = factor(month),
         low_vis = as.integer(visibility_km < 5))

logit <- glm(dep_del15 ~ hour_block + month + carrier + any_precip + snow +
               fog_mist + low_vis + wind_speed_ms,
             data = logit_data, family = binomial)

broom::tidy(logit) %>%
  filter(term %in% c("any_precip", "snow", "fog_mist", "low_vis",
                     "wind_speed_ms")) %>%
  transmute(Variable = recode(term, any_precip = "Any precipitation",
                              snow = "Snow (in addition)",
                              fog_mist = "Fog or mist",
                              low_vis = "Visibility < 5 km",
                              wind_speed_ms = "Wind speed (per m/s)"),
            `Odds ratio` = exp(estimate),
            `95% CI low` = exp(estimate - 1.96 * std.error),
            `95% CI high` = exp(estimate + 1.96 * std.error),
            `p-value` = pvalue(p.value)) %>%
  knitr::kable(format = "latex", booktabs = TRUE, digits = 3,
               caption = paste("Adjusted odds ratios of a 15+ minute",
                               "delay for weather variables, from a logistic",
                               "regression that also includes departure-time",
                               "block, month and carrier."))
```
